title: Time I: the clock, the calendar, and plain past た

grammarPoints.rule: Past ten, Japanese counts by ARITHMETIC. Stack a digit on the RIGHT of じゅう and you add: じゅう + ご = じゅうご (15). Stack a digit on the LEFT and you multiply: さん + じゅう = さんじゅう (30), よん + じゅう = よんじゅう (40), ご + じゅう = ごじゅう (50), なな + じゅう = ななじゅう (70). Combine both for everything in between: ろくじゅうご = 65. There is nothing new to memorise — you already know every piece.

antiPattern.why: ten on its own is just じゅう — いちじゅう is not a number

grammarPoints.rule: A clock hour is the number plus 〜じ. Three readings break the pattern and are simply learned: 4 is よじ (never よんじ), 7 is しちじ (never ななじ), 9 is くじ (never きゅうじ). なんじ asks 'what time?', and はん after the hour means half past — ごじはん is 5:30.

examples.ja: いちじ にじ さんじ よじ
ごじ ろくじ しちじ はちじ

antiPattern.why: four o'clock is よじ — よん never takes 〜じ

grammarPoints.rule: A point on the CLOCK takes に: さんじに いく. It is the same に you already use for a destination — Japanese treats a moment in time like a place you arrive at. Words that are not clock readings take NO に at all: きょう いく, あした いく. ごぜん (a.m.) and ごご (p.m.) sit in front of the hour: ごご さんじに.

antiPattern.why: a clock time needs に — さんじに いく

grammarPoints.rule: Plain past is た, and it runs on the SAME sound-change table you bought for て. Swap て for た and で for だ, and you are done. る-verbs: たべる → たべた. う-verbs: む/ぶ/ぬ → んだ (のむ → のんだ); う/つ/る → った (かう → かった); く → いた (きく → きいた); ぐ → いだ. する → した, くる → きた, and いく is the same rebel it was for て: いった. A past sentence usually opens with the time it happened: きのう is 'yesterday', so きのう のんだ is 'I drank it yesterday'.

antiPattern.why: のむ ends in む, so it joins the んだ group — のんだ, not のみた

grammarPoints.rule: The same three verbs that broke the て table break this one, in the same way: する → した, くる → きた, and いく → いった, never いいた. That is the whole exception list — every other verb you know follows the rows. わかる is regular (わかった) but drill it here anyway; you will reach for it constantly.

antiPattern.why: いく ends in く but skips the く→いた row — its past is いった.

grammarPoints.rule: だ has a past cell too, and it is だった: ねこだ → ねこだった. Verbs take た, nouns take だった — the same split you already know from the present, where a verb stands alone and a noun needs だ. Its polite twin is でした, which arrives beside ました.

examples.ja: それは ねこだった。
きのうは じゅぎょうだった。

antiPattern.why: nouns take だった — た alone is for verbs

grammarPoints.rule: The polite past swaps ます for ました — same stem, different tail. のみます → のみました. Nothing else moves: ました is the polite skin on the た you just learned. Plain た goes to friends; ました goes to teachers, staff and strangers.

examples.ja: みずを のみました。
ごはんを たべました。
みせに いきました。

antiPattern.ja: みずを のみますた。
antiPattern.why: ました REPLACES ます — you never stack た on top of it

grammarPoints.rule: いつ asks WHEN. It stands where a time word would stand and takes no particle of its own: いつ いく？ Answer with any time at all — さんじに, きょう, きのう, ごご. なんじ is the narrow version: it asks for a reading on the clock, so its answer is always an hour.

antiPattern.why: いつ takes no に — the particle belongs to a clock time, not to the question word
